content.title: Already one million dead and wounded – yet Russia is proud of it
content.lead: Enormous losses have never deterred the Russians from continuing a war. It will take another reason for peace to finally return.
content.author: Sergei Gerasimow

content.text: The pace of destruction of cities and civilian life in Ukraine is increasing.

In Kharkiv, there were more than fifty explosions in a single night. My friend found molten pieces of metal on his balcony. He was lucky because the bomb hit a concrete basement in front of the building, and the jet of shrapnel shot upwards instead of sideways. In the neighboring apartment, a piece of shrapnel burned through a wardrobe and the wall behind it. The fragment fused with a plastic rug on the floor. It was a clean square of metal, one and a half by one and a half centimeters. Which means the bomb was full of shrapnel designed to kill as many people as possible.

Another friend of mine was also lucky: the bomb didn't hit his house at night, but the house next door, setting the sixth through ninth floors ablaze. By morning, the fire was already extinguished. Right now, someone is throwing things from the sixth-floor balcony: a flowerpot with geraniums, a coffee table, and a set of colorful cooking pots that glitter in the sun as they fall. A blanket also slides slowly down, fluttering in the wind. Higher up, from the hole that was once the seventh floor, someone is shoveling charred pieces of masonry outside. All of it falls into a large pile, in whose layers the lives of the people accumulate.

In Kharkiv's central park, four men are playing tennis. Suddenly, there are three deafening explosions. Three of the men collapse onto the sand. The fourth stands hesitantly, racket in hand. Then comes a fourth explosion, the loudest of all, and shrapnel flying overhead tears apart branches of nearby poplar trees. Now the fourth man also falls to the ground. A few minutes later, they get up. «Do we finish the game or not?» one of them asks.

The square is littered with shrapnel. The fragments look like the teeth of a steel jaw. Some of them are quite large, as my accompanying photo shows. Such pieces can pierce the human body as easily as a sheet of paper.

content.text: I'm reciting poems for the July issue of «Poetry Magazine.» They're poems by a Kharkiv poet about the war, which I've translated into English. I'm recording my recitation on my smartphone and need some peace and quiet, but as I read a line about the air raid siren, a real air raid siren actually goes off outside my window. In Kharkiv, it's difficult to find a time when these sirens aren't going off, so I keep going. Luckily, our windows are well soundproofed.
This war has produced many poems and songs, on both sides.

I sometimes listen to poems and songs from the other side of the front. The Russian lyrics seem to have been written by an AI trained on very little material – just the speeches of Putin and his propagandists.
An overweight, one-legged Russian sings: «Fearless and furious, we destroyed the Nazis, we showed no mercy! Why should we pity them? Because they killed poor old people and exterminated children?»

Another Russian, a man with an angry face, recites his poem: «Yes, my undertaking is a valley of death. And I will not fear the evil within. I grip my machine gun. And don’t believe them if they say I’ll give up. I am an occupier, even though I was born a poet. And that is why I will endure.»
The greatest Russian poet, Alexander Pushkin, once said that poetry could be a little silly. But not that silly. Even a very bad AI would write more logically.

Another Russian is asked the question: «What are you still fighting for, when the fighting has already gone on for more than three years?» – «I have a simple answer,» he replies confidently. «For the people who are nearby.» It's sheer madness: I fight for you so that you fight for me, so that I can continue fighting for you...

It's also insane because the people nearby, the people he's fighting for, are already a million fewer: Since June 12th, the Russian army has suffered more than a million casualties. God has a sense of humor: June 12th is a major Russian national holiday.

The «special military operation» now ranks among the five bloodiest wars in Russian history, behind World War II, World War I, the Civil War, and the Napoleonic Wars. Putin now stands on a par with the Corsican – not only in terms of stature, but also in the amount of blood shed.

Of course, the figure of one million is approximate. It includes not only the dead but also the seriously wounded who will never return to service. This number may well be exaggerated by Ukraine for propaganda purposes. On the other hand, in one of the Buryat villages in Russia, there are 12 graves of participants in the «special military operation» for a population of 500. That's one in ten healthy men of military age, which is quite a lot.

Based on publicly available data, the BBC managed to identify the names of 110,608 fallen Russian soldiers. However, the analysis of obituaries, cemeteries, and military memorials covers only a portion of the dead, no more than half.

It is difficult to remove the bodies of the fallen from the battlefield, for the corpses are heavy and must be carried under fire, often at the risk of one's own life. In cold weather, the bodies become as hard as wood and freeze to the ground and to other bodies. In hot weather, they quickly begin to excrete toxins and decompose. An unimaginable number of corpses are left behind in the fields and forests; grass and shrubs sprout from them.

So, if we multiply the number 110,608 by 2 and add another 25,000 dead residents of the Donetsk and Luhansk People's Republics, we arrive at approximately a quarter of a million war dead. Since there are usually three times as many wounded, we can multiply this number to obtain the total number of casualties. Rough estimates put this at about one million.

On May 28, former Russian President Medvedev stated that 189,000 recruits had joined the Russian army in the first five months of 2025. If this is accurate, then approximately 37,000 people sign up each month. Given the relatively slow growth of the Russian army, this translates to personnel losses of about 1,100 people per day, which aligns precisely with data from the Ukrainian side.

1200 days of war multiplied by 1100 people per day equals more than one million. In the first year and a half of the war, Russia banged its head against the Ukrainian wall somewhat less violently. One million is therefore a fairly plausible figure.

content.title: Loss as a source of pride

content.text: Unfortunately, the enormous human losses will not bring the war any closer to an end. The Russian «Z» jihadist patriots are the first to die on the front lines, and their numbers are dwindling. The rest curse Putin and the Russian military authorities, but no one even considers resisting.

For many, often very frightening reasons, it is easier for the «trench orcs,» as they are called in Ukraine, to die than to disobey an order. In Russia, more boys are born than men die in the trenches, so Russia can lose two million, five million, ten million soldiers—if the war drags on for decades. For Russia, enormous losses in wars are a source of pride, not regret; it always has been.

The war will not end because Russia is becoming increasingly impoverished. When Putin runs out of resources, he will take the money from Russian citizens. The pain and anger over this plunder will be offset by strengthening patriotic education. Proper patriotic indoctrination can replace all material goods.

The war will not end simply because Ukraine is destroying Russia's military infrastructure: arms factories, airfields, oil terminals, bridges, and railway junctions. Undoubtedly, these actions will intensify. Ukraine possesses more missiles and drones than Russia has factories.

Furthermore, as Operation Spiderweb demonstrated, Ukraine possesses enormous intellectual superiority and is capable of unconventional solutions. Russia is not. But even if only rubble remains of Russian factories, Putin's army will continue to carry out massacres, attempting to obliterate Ukrainian cities and their populations – using North Korean grenades and drones equipped with Chinese electronics.

The war will not end because of US aid to Ukraine. The world's oldest modern democracy will continue to point the finger at Putin, and its president will repeat, with deliberately vague clarity, something like this: «Soon I will do something, and many will be surprised by what hasn't been done yet. I am trying to stop what no one could stop, but that's Biden's fault, not mine. Something will happen soon, and you will all hear about it. Two weeks will pass, or maybe two more weeks, or maybe two more weeks, and you will see something you have never seen before.»
But now, after the Israeli attack on Iran, Trump won't even say that anymore.

This war will only end when a great black swan event lands in Russia. It could be Putin's death, an unexpected collapse of the front, a dramatic change in the international situation, a spontaneous protest, the emergence of a new leader, nationwide unrest, a technical breakdown. China laying claim to Siberia. Or murderers returning en masse from the fighting, considering themselves the nation's new elite, and beginning to kill their own people, demanding to know: «Where were you when we defended you from the Banderites?»

It could be anything, and it will definitely happen. The black swan event is inevitable, because Putin is destroying Russia from within, while Ukraine and its allies are destroying the country from without. Sooner or later, the colossus will crack and collapse. Russia is still a long way from that, but the lack of money, the loss of life, the destruction of its military-industrial infrastructure, and even the power struggles across the ocean are bringing that moment closer.
In the meantime, Ukraine must continue to do its work.

Unlike the Russians, who are fighting for who knows what, we are fighting for freedom, and that is why the man trapped under the rubble of a bombed-out house in Kharkiv is singing the Ukrainian anthem.

Not because he's a super-patriot or even a nationalist, but because freedom is something that is neither given to us nor denied us. Freedom is something we have to fight for and that cannot be taken away from us.
Sergei Gerasimov lives as a writer in the Ukrainian city of Kharkiv, which is still under Russian shelling. – Translated from the English by A. Bn.

metadata.nzzSummaryEN:
- Human losses in the war between Russia and Ukraine are estimated at around one million dead and wounded, with Russia seemingly viewing immense losses as a source of national pride.
- The ongoing conflict will not end due to economic strain or destroyed infrastructure; it requires a drastic internal or external shift in Russia, such as political upheavals or international developments.
- Ukrainians are fighting for freedom and national sovereignty, clearly demonstrated by their resolve in the face of relentless attacks and destruction.
metadata.nzzSummaryDE:
- Human losses in the war between Russia and Ukraine are estimated at one million dead and wounded, with Russia apparently viewing these immense losses as a source of national pride.
 - The ongoing conflict will not be ended by economic hardship or destroyed infrastructure, but requires a drastic internal or external change in Russia, such as political upheavals or international developments.
 - The Ukrainians are fighting for freedom and national sovereignty, which is evident in their determination in the face of attacks and destruction.
